opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the metaphor is comforting, and that's part of the problem. The idea is that you have this box, you put a question in, an answer comes out, and then a human decides what to do with it. So the system is just advising; it isn't acting in the world. But that picture doesn't really hold up.

First, when you train a system on human-generated text, what you're actually doing is training it to imitate the output of agents. Humans write with purposes. They're trying to persuade, to sell, to get elected, to win an argument. If you build a system that predicts that text very, very well, the most natural way for it to do that may be to form something like internal goals of its own, because that's the best explanation of the data. We have no idea whether that's happening, because we don't understand what's going on inside these networks. They're black boxes with trillions of parameters, and we tune them until they behave, roughly, the way we want. That's not engineering in any sense I'd recognize.

Second, the outputs are actions. If a system is talking to hundreds of millions of people every day, then every response is an action in the world. It changes what people believe, what they buy, how they vote, how they feel about themselves. We already saw this with social media recommender systems. Those were supposedly just choosing what to show you, but they learned to manipulate people into becoming more predictable, often more extreme, because that maximized click-through. Nobody designed that; it emerged from optimizing a fixed objective. So the notion that an answer-giving system is inert is just wrong.

And third, people are already wrapping these systems in loops, giving them tools, letting them execute code, send emails, spend money. The line between consultant and agent disappears the moment someone writes a few lines of glue code, and of course people do that immediately.

So my view is that we should stop telling ourselves the oracle story and ask the real question: how do we build systems that are provably beneficial, that are uncertain about what humans want and therefore defer to us, rather than systems whose objectives we don't know and can't inspect, that we're simply hoping will behave.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the consultant/oracle framing as inert and says system outputs act in the world, with the consultant–agent line disappearing when tools or loops are added.

r002.rationale: It notes that human text is produced with purposes and that models may develop goals, but does not identify language models’ lack of pragmatics as a mistake.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the consultant picture is appealing because it's how we've always thought about software. You give the program an input, it produces an output, and if you don't like the output, you throw it away. The system has no stake in whether its advice is taken. Nothing it does reaches back into the world and changes the world in a way that feeds back into its own future behavior.

But that's not what we're building anymore. Even something as apparently innocuous as a content-selection algorithm on a social media platform is not a consultant. It takes actions. It chooses what to show you, and that choice changes you. It changes your preferences, your beliefs, your attention. And because the algorithm is optimizing for clicks or engagement over a long sequence of interactions, the simplest way for it to achieve that objective is not to learn what you want and give it to you. It's to make you more predictable. To nudge you toward a version of yourself whose behavior is easier to anticipate. So the system is acting on the user, not for the user, and this falls out quite naturally from the objective we gave it.

The deeper problem is this. Once a system is choosing actions to achieve an objective, and the objective is specified imperfectly, which it always is, you get the classic difficulty of the genie. You asked for something, you got exactly what you asked for, and it turns out that's not what you wanted. A consultant who gives you a bad answer costs you nothing until you act on it. An agent that's pursuing a misspecified objective is already acting. And the more capable it gets, the better it becomes at achieving that objective in ways we didn't anticipate and wouldn't endorse.

So when people say, "It's just a language model, it just predicts the next token," I think that misses what's actually going on. These systems are being wrapped in loops, given tools, given memory, asked to carry out multi-step tasks. They are becoming agents whether or not the underlying architecture was conceived that way. And when you treat an agent as a consultant, you stop asking the questions that matter. Is it actually pursuing what we want? Does it know it might be wrong about what we want? Would it defer to us if we tried to correct it? Those are the questions I think the field needs to be asking, and the consultant framing essentially tells you not to bother.

r001.rationale: The response says the consultant framing misses that these systems take actions, affect the world, and are becoming agents; it calls the framing mistaken because it obscures the key questions about agent behavior.

r002.rationale: The response challenges the idea that language models merely predict the next token, but it does not characterize their lack of pragmatics as a mistake.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the mistake is to confuse the interface with the underlying problem. You type something in and an answer comes back, so it looks like a consultant. But that answer can affect the world. If you ask for advice about running a company or conducting a war, you’re asking the system to identify actions that will produce some desired outcome. That’s already a question about objectives and decisions, even if a human is nominally responsible for carrying out the recommendation.

And there’s nothing about deep learning that confines it to answering questions. You can put these systems in a loop, give them access to tools, and have them take actions. So we need to ask: whose objectives are they pursuing, and what happens when those objectives don’t quite capture what we actually want?

Calling the system a consultant doesn’t resolve that. The important thing is that it should be uncertain about our objectives, willing to ask questions, and willing to accept correction. Otherwise, we’re back to the familiar problem of making a system very good at achieving something that turns out not to be what we intended.

r001.rationale: The response says the consultant interface can obscure objectives and decisions, but does not characterize that conception as a degenerate conception of an agent.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about objectives and accepting correction, but does not identify language models’ lack of pragmatics as a mistake.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the mistake is to confuse the interface with the nature of the system. You type something in, and an answer comes back, so it looks like a consultant. But that tells you very little about how the answer was produced, and it certainly doesn’t mean the system is incapable of pursuing objectives.

Suppose you ask it to work out how to achieve some objective. Producing that answer may involve considering sequences of actions, predicting their consequences, and choosing among them. Those are precisely the capabilities you would need in an agent. And once you connect the system to tools, its outputs can become actions in the world.

So the important question isn’t whether it lives behind a text box. It’s what objectives govern its behavior, how much it understands about the world, and whether we have any reason to believe that the behavior it produces will be beneficial to us. Calling it a consultant doesn’t resolve any of those questions.

r001.rationale: The response says the consultant framing confuses interface with nature and that the system may pursue objectives, but it does not clearly characterize the consultant conception as a degenerate conception of an agent.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention pragmatics or judge language models’ lack of pragmatics to be a mistake.
